  • Inverting IRIS Observations with MART

Inverting IRIS Observations with MART#

The main target of ESIS-I is the \(\text{O\,\textsc{v}}\;630\,\AA\) spectral line. To our knowledge, high-quality spectroheliograms of this line are not available to use as a test dataset. The Coronal Diagnostic Spectrometer (CDS) [Harrison et al., 1996] and the Solar Ultraviolet Measurements of Emitted Radiation (SUMER) [Wilhelm et al., 1995] have both observed this line, but their spatial or spectral resolution is not sufficient to use as a test for ESIS. Instead, we will use observations of the \(\text{Si\,\textsc{iv}}\;1394\,\AA\) spectral line from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) [De Pontieu et al., 2014] as a proxy for the \(\text{O\,\textsc{v}}\;630\,\AA\) line. These observations will be used along with a simple model of the ESIS instrument to create synthetic ESIS images. We will then use MART to invert these images and test how well it recovers the original scene.

Loading the Test Scene#

Load an IRIS observation to use as a test scene to invert. This function shifts and scales the \(\text{Si\,\textsc{iv}}\;1394\,\AA\) spectral line observed by IRIS to match the \(\text{O\,\textsc{v}}\;630\,\AA\) line observed by ESIS.

%%time
scene = esis.flights.f1.data.synth.scene_iris(
    time_start="2014-07-04 11:40",
    velocity_max=150 * u.km / u.s,
)

Wall time: 28.2 s

Defining a Model of the ESIS Instrument#

In this tutorial we’ll use an idealized version of the ESIS instrument model that considers only dispersion and shot noise.

We’ll start by saving the rest wavelength of the \(\text{O}\,\textsc{v}\;630\,\AA\) line.

[8]:

wavelength_rest = scene.inputs.wavelength_rest

Use the rest wavelength to define an astropy.units equivalency for converting between Doppler velocities and wavelength units.

[9]:

AA = dict(unit=u.AA, equivalencies=u.doppler_optical(wavelength_rest))

Use the coordinates of the scene as the coordinates of the reconstructed scene.

[10]:

coordinates_scene = scene.inputs

Define the vertices of the pixel grid on the sensor.

[11]:

position_sensor = na.Cartesian2dVectorArray(
    x=na.arange(0, 300 + 1, axis="sensor_x") * u.pix,
    y=na.arange(0, 300 + 1, axis="sensor_y") * u.pix,
)
Use these vertices to form the sensor coordinates by combining it with the wavelength coordinates of the scene.
[12]:

coordinates_sensor = na.SpectralPositionalVectorArray(
    wavelength=scene.inputs.wavelength,
    position=position_sensor,
)

Define the dispersion angles of the simulated ESIS instrument and add an arbitrary offset so that the dispersion directions are not aligned with the pixel grid of the scene.

[13]:

angle = na.linspace(0, 180, num=4, axis="channel", endpoint=False) * u.deg
angle = angle + 0.4 * u.rad
angle.ndarray

[13]:
$[22.918312,~67.918312,~112.91831,~157.91831]\mathrm{{}^{\circ}}$

Define a unique string for each channel.

[14]:

channel = "dispersion angle = " + angle.to_string_array("%03d")

Compute the effective area of ESIS using values from the instrument paper draft.

[15]:

ccd = optika.sensors.materials.e2v_ccd97()
absorbance = ccd.absorbance(
    wavelength=wavelength_rest,
    normal=na.Cartesian3dVectorArray(0, 0, -1),
).average
area_effective = 4 * u.mm ** 2 / 0.39 * absorbance.ndarray
area_effective

[15]:
$5.5899989 \; \mathrm{mm^{2}}$

Define the name of the logical axis representing the different channels of the ESIS instrument.

[16]:

axis_channel = "channel"

Using the values we computed above, construct a model of the ESIS instrument.

[17]:

instrument = ctis.instruments.IdealInstrument(
    area_effective=area_effective,
    timedelta_exposure=10 * u.s,
    plate_scale=0.77 * u.arcsec / u.pix,
    dispersion=((17.5 * u.km / u.s).to(**AA) - wavelength_rest) / u.pix,
    angle=angle,
    wavelength_ref=wavelength_rest,
    position_ref=na.Cartesian2dVectorArray(150, 150) * u.pix,
    coordinates_scene=coordinates_scene,
    coordinates_sensor=coordinates_sensor,
    channel=channel,
    axis_channel=axis_channel,
    axis_wavelength=scene.axis_wavelength,
    axis_scene_xy=(scene.axis_detector_x, scene.axis_detector_y),
    axis_sensor_xy=("sensor_x", "sensor_y"),
)

Create synthetic ESIS images#

To calculate synthetic images, all we need to do is apply the image() method to the IRIS observation we prepared.

Display all four synthetic images.
[19]:

with astropy.visualization.quantity_support():
    fig, axs = na.plt.subplots(
        axis_rows="rows",
        axis_cols="cols",
        nrows=2,
        ncols=2,
        constrained_layout=True,
        figsize=(10,9),
        sharex=True,
        sharey=True,
        origin="upper",
    )
    ax = axs.combine_axes(("rows", "cols"), axis_channel)
    norm = matplotlib.colors.PowerNorm(
        gamma=0.5,
        vmin=0,
        vmax=images.outputs.value.percentile(99.9).ndarray,
    )
    colorizer = plt.Colorizer(
        cmap="gray",
        norm=norm,
    )
    img = na.plt.pcolormesh(
        # channel,
        images.inputs.position.x,
        images.inputs.position.y,
        C=images.outputs.value,
        ax=ax,
        colorizer=colorizer,
    )
    plt.colorbar(
        mappable=plt.cm.ScalarMappable(colorizer=colorizer),
        ax=ax.ndarray,
        label=f"signal ({images.outputs.unit:latex_inline})",
    )
    na.plt.set_title(channel, ax=ax)
    na.plt.set_aspect("equal", ax=ax)
    na.plt.set_xlabel(f"sensor $x$ ({images.inputs.position.x.unit})", ax=axs[dict(rows=~0)])
    na.plt.set_ylabel(f"sensor $y$ ({images.inputs.position.y.unit})", ax=axs[dict(cols=0)])

Invert synthetic ESIS images#

Now for the tricky part, inverting these images into a reconstructed scene using MART. An important part of using MART effectively is the initial guess supplied to the algorithm.

spectrum_avg = scene.outputs.mean((scene.axis_detector_x, scene.axis_detector_y))
spectrum_avg = spectrum_avg / spectrum_avg.sum()

[35]:

std_OV = esis.flights.f1.spectrum.O_V.width_doppler
v = scene.inputs.velocity.cell_centers(scene.axis_wavelength)
# guess_spectral = np.exp(-np.square(v / std_OV) / 2)
std_OV = 37.5  * 1.5 * u.km / u.s
kappa = 0.2
v0 = 0 * u.km / u.s
guess_spectral = (1 + np.square((v - v0) / std_OV) / kappa)**(-kappa - 1)
guess_spectral = guess_spectral / guess_spectral.sum()

[36]:

guess_spatial.sum()
